title: Like an infant
hook: can you soften your breath like a baby's? give birth without possessing (Tao Te Ching 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter nine: a cup filled to the brim, and the advice to stop before it spills. Did you stop one thing early? What did you leave in the cup? Day one thousand seventy-two.

A baby asleep on a parent's chest. Watch the belly, not the face. It rises, it falls, and nothing in the rest of the body seems to be helping or fighting. No clenched jaw. No shoulders up near the ears. Now check your own breath, right where it is, without fixing it. Is it soft, or is it working? Chapter ten of the Tao Te Ching holds up that sleeping baby as a kind of teacher. And this chapter doesn't instruct. It asks.
screen: `A BABY ASLEEP.` → `WATCH THE BELLY.` → `CHAPTER TEN ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, the chapter is a string of questions. Can you hold body and spirit together, and not let them drift apart? Can you gather your breath and make it soft, like an infant's? Can you wipe your inner sight clean? Can you care for people without cleverness? Line after line ends in a question, and the chapter doesn't answer them. They're left open, the way a teacher might leave a hard question on the board overnight. Second, why an infant? A baby hasn't learned to brace yet. It hasn't learned to hold its breath before a hard conversation or to tighten up in traffic. The softness isn't a technique it practiced; it simply hasn't been trained out of it. The chapter seems to ask whether a grown person can find their way back to that, on purpose. Third, softness here isn't weakness. Two days ago, chapter eight praised water for doing good without competing. A soft breath has the same quiet strength, small enough to carry in your own chest. Fourth, the chapter turns from breath to how a person treats what they make. It closes with a list: to give life and not possess it, to act and not lean on it, to lead and not control. The book calls this a hidden kind of virtue. A parent knows the shape of it: you raise a child, and the child is not yours to own. The soft breath and the open hand belong to the same chapter, side by side.
screen: `A CHAPTER OF QUESTIONS.` · `A BABY HASN'T LEARNED TO BRACE.` · `SOFT ISN'T WEAK.` · `GIVE LIFE, AND DON'T POSSESS IT.` · then, large: `CAN YOU MAKE YOUR BREATH SOFT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a few minutes of soft breath. Sit or lie down, and put one hand on your belly. Let the breath come in without pulling it, and go out without pushing it. If you notice bracing, in the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, let that one place go. You're not trying to breathe slowly or deeply. Only softly, the way the sleeping baby does. When a thought pulls you away, come back to the hand rising and falling. The bell holds the time.
Like an infant. Chapter ten's picture for a breath that isn't bracing against anything, and a life that gives without holding on. Today's word.
Your line: soft breath. Pick one tense moment today, a message, a line, a meeting, and before it starts, check your breath and let it soften once. Day one thousand seventy-two.

howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching pair chapter ten with a few minutes of quiet, unforced breathing, letting the breath move on its own instead of controlling it.

original.note: Chinese, from the Tao Te Ching: an infant, a baby. Chapter ten asks if the breath can become soft like one.

trapdoor: what you thought: like an infant means being naive.
what it means: a breath and a body that haven't learned to brace, and a way of giving life without possessing it.
what a scholar hears: the chapter is built as questions, and its closing list (give life, don't possess; lead, don't control) names a hidden virtue.

notes: Chapter 10 paraphrased throughout (no quotation): the questions about holding body and spirit as one, softening the breath like an infant, cleansing inner vision, and caring for people without cleverness; and the closing list (produce without possessing, act without relying, lead without controlling), called 'mysterious virtue' (玄德), rendered here as 'a hidden kind of virtue'.
